Racing the Data: An LLM-Assisted Exploratory Analysis of the 2024 NYC Marathon

Manuel Rodriguez Berdud
mrodriguezberdud318@floridapoly.edu
DW & EDA Spring 2026

Introduction and Motivation

Marathon datasets are ideal for exploratory analysis because they combine athletic performance, demographics, and geography at very large scale. In events like the New York City Marathon, tens of thousands of runners of different ages, genders, and nationalities finish the same race under comparable conditions. This makes the dataset useful for studying broad performance patterns while also preserving individual-level variation.

The 2024 NYC Marathon Finishers dataset, obtained from Data Is Plural, contains detailed records (e.g., finishing times, pace, rankings, age, sex, and location) and more than 55,000 observations. Beyond sports analytics, this type of data is valuable for understanding participation trends, fairness across age groups, and the global composition of a major endurance event.

At the same time, extracting insight from this data depends heavily on data wrangling quality. Real-world race tables include non-standard time formats, missing geographic values, and categorical inconsistencies that must be fixed before doing any analysis, visualizations or summaries. In practice, these cleaning and transformation steps consume a large share of the analysis workflow.

This project is motivated by a practical question: can LLMs improve the speed and quality of exploratory data preparation without replacing statistical rigor? Instead of treating models as black-box decision makers, the workflow uses LLMs as assistants for transformation design, feature ideation, and hypothesis generation, while all final computations and checks remain in R.

The project therefore has two complementary goals:

  1. Produce a rigorous EDA of NYC Marathon performance trends (age, experience, and geography).
  2. Evaluate how LLM-assisted wrangling contributes to a transparent, reproducible analysis pipeline.

By combining domain-focused marathon questions with process-focused evaluation of LLM assistance, the report aims to show both substantive findings and methodological lessons for data wrangling practice.

Related Work

The literature relevant to this project can be grouped into two streams: (1) LLM-enabled data wrangling and (2) marathon participation/performance analysis.

In the first stream, Jaimovitch-Lopez et al. provide foundational evidence that language models can automate parts of wrangling pipelines such as type inference, canonicalization, anomaly handling, and transformation from examples. Their results show clear promise, while also emphasizing reliability limits and the need for human validation in high-stakes cleaning decisions (Jaimovitch-López et al. 2023).

Recent work extends this direction toward operational systems. AutoDW proposes an LLM-centered architecture for reducing manual scripting in repetitive wrangling tasks, highlighting practical integration patterns for analysts (Liu et al. 2024). Additional evidence from code-generating LLM studies shows that models can assist in automating transformation logic, but output quality still depends strongly on prompt design and post-generation verification (Akella and Narayanam 2025).

At the synthesis level, Zhou et al. survey application-ready LLM data preparation methods across cleaning, integration, and enrichment, and identify a broader shift from rigid rule-based pipelines to context-aware, prompt-driven workflows (Zhou et al. 2025). This survey is especially relevant for framing this project as an applied, human-in-the-loop EDA workflow rather than full automation.

The second stream focuses on marathon data itself. Jokl et al. examined master-level performance in NYC Marathon results, showing how age stratification can reveal meaningful differences in long-term endurance outcomes (Jokl, Sethi, and Cooper 2004). Vitti et al. analyzed approximately 1.2 million NYC Marathon records across fifty years, documenting participation and performance trends at population scale (Vitti et al. 2019). Hunter and Stevens further quantified sex differences in marathon performance at advanced ages, reinforcing the need for demographic-aware interpretation of raw finishing times (Hunter and Stevens 2013).

Together, these two streams motivate the design of this study: marathon analytics provides rich domain questions, while LLM wrangling research provides methods for accelerating preparation and hypothesis generation. The key addressed here is the combination of both perspectives in a single reproducible workflow, where LLM assistance is used explicitly but all outputs are validated through R-based analysis.

Dataset Description and Source

The raw dataset contains official individual-level finisher results from the 2024 New York City Marathon. Data access was facilitated through Data Is Plural, while the underlying official source is New York Road Runners (NYRR) race results (New York Road Runners 2024).

The file is stored in Excel format and includes core runner attributes, rankings, and timing fields. In the raw table, the variables are primarily:

  • Identifiers and demographics: runnerId, firstName, bib, age, gender
  • Geography: city, stateProvince, countryCode, iaaf
  • Performance and ranking outcomes: overallPlace, genderPlace, ageGradePlace, ageGradePercent, racesCount
  • Time-based variables: overallTime, pace, ageGradeTime

This structure makes the dataset especially useful for Exploratory Data Analysis because it supports multiple analytical levels simultaneously: absolute performance (finish time), relative performance (age-grade measures), subgroup comparisons (age, sex, geography, and experience).

After inspecting the raw dataset for the first time, I identified practical issues that directly motivate the cleaning pipeline:

  1. Time variables are recorded in clock-style format (hh:mm:ss) and require conversion to numeric minutes for valid aggregation and plotting.
  2. A small set of records appears with firstName == "Anonymous" and effectively empty identifying information, requiring row-level filtering.
  3. Geographic fields (city, stateProvince) contain missing values, which are handled with an explicit Unknown category to avoid fabricated imputations.

The first few rows of raw observations are shown below:

Data Wrangling

This section is designed to clean, filter, and enrich the 2024 NYC Marathon Results raw dataset using Large Language Models (mainly using Copilot in Visual Study Code). For better structure, the data wrangling tasks are divided into two main categories:

  1. Data cleaning

  2. Data Enrichment

Task 1: Data cleaning

  1. Data Standardization

The OverallTime, Pace, and ageGradeTime columns are formatted as hh:mm:ss. We want to standardize these variables so they are all represented in minutes:

nyc_marathon_cleaned <- nyc_marathon %>%
  mutate(
    OverallTime_min = round(
      hour(overallTime) * 60 +
      minute(overallTime) +
      second(overallTime) / 60,
      2),
    Pace_min = round(
      hour(pace) + minute(pace) / 60,
      2),
    ageGradeTime_min = round(
      hour(ageGradeTime) + minute(ageGradeTime) / 60,
      2)
  ) %>%
  select(-overallTime, -pace, -ageGradeTime) # dropping original columns

Handling missing values:

We find a “pattern” on the amount of missing values for some of the variables. After inspection, I found that there are 12 rows of observations with no values at all (firstName = “Anonymous”).

nyc_marathon_cleaned <- nyc_marathon_cleaned %>% filter(

)

After inspection, missing values for both variables are replaced with the category Unknown. Since these variables represent geographic identifiers, imputing values would introduce artificial location information.

nyc_marathon_cleaned <- nyc_marathon_cleaned %>% mutate(
  city = ifelse(is.na(city), "Unknown", city),
  stateProvince = ifelse(is.na(stateProvince), "Unknown", stateProvince)
)

  1. Filtering Data

In this dataset, there are some variables that won´t be useful for the upcoming analysis. Thus, I have decided to remove them. These features are:

  • runnerId: this variable doesn´t provide any good information for my study.

  • iaaf: since the dataset already provides countryCode, I don´t need to include this other feature that explains the same thing.

nyc_marathon_cleaned <- nyc_marathon_cleaned %>% select(
  -runnerId,
  -iaaf
)

The summary() function revealed that racesCount has a maximum value of 1,393. This initially appeared anomalous, suggesting one participant had run the NYC Marathon 1,393 times. Upon investigation, I discovered that this feature represents the total number of races completed through the New York Road Runners system (not just the NYC Marathon), which hosts over 10 races annually. This finding prompted me to correct the metadata documentation to clarify the true scope of this variable.

  1. Data Annotation

Generating metadata for documentation. Considering both the raw and cleaned datasets. The code generated is later used for the data README.md

  1. Feature Engineering

Adding extra features that will be beneficial for analysis. They explain age, level, and experience categories better:

  • age_group: lifecycle stage by age

  • runner_exp: experience level based on total number of races the runner has completed in the NYRR race system (racesCount)

  • Type_of_runner: performance level based on AgeGradePercentage

# age group feature:
# Purpose: group runners into interpretable age bands for cohort analysis and comparisons.

nyc_marathon_cleaned <- nyc_marathon_cleaned %>%
    mutate(
      age_group = case_when(
        age < 20 ~ "Under 20",
        age >= 20 & age < 30 ~ "20-29",
        age >= 30 & age < 40 ~ "30-39",
        age >= 40 & age < 50 ~ "40-49",
        age >= 50 & age < 60 ~ "50-59",
        age >= 60 ~ "Over 60",
        TRUE ~ NA_character_
      )
    )

# ---------------

# Experience in the NYC Marathon feature: 
# Purpose: classify runners by prior race participation volume

nyc_marathon_cleaned <- nyc_marathon_cleaned %>%
    mutate(
      runner_exp = case_when(
        racesCount <= 1 ~ "First-time runner",
        racesCount >= 2 & racesCount <= 4 ~ "Experienced runner",
        racesCount >= 5 & racesCount <= 10 ~ "Golden runner",
        racesCount > 10 ~ "Master runner",
        TRUE ~ NA_character_
      )
    )

# ----------------

# Type of runner feature:
# Purpose: segment runners by standardized performance quality

nyc_marathon_cleaned <- nyc_marathon_cleaned %>%
    mutate(
      age_grade_value = as.numeric(gsub("%", "", as.character(ageGradePercent))),
      Type_of_runner = case_when(
        age_grade_value >= 85 ~ "Elite",
        age_grade_value >= 75 & age_grade_value < 85 ~ "Professional",
        age_grade_value >= 60 & age_grade_value < 75 ~ "Competitive",
        age_grade_value < 60 ~ "Recreational",
        TRUE ~ NA_character_
      )
    ) %>%
    select(-age_grade_value)

Exploratory Data Analysis

After data wrangling, a cleaner dataset is used for Exploratory Data Analysis. In this section, we focus on answering three of our top research questions:

  1. Age and performance:
  • when do runners achieve peak performance?
  • how do older runners compare to younger runners relative to age group?
  1. Experience and performance:
  • does prior race experience correspond to better finish times and age-graded results?
  1. Geographic patterns:
  • how international is the NYC Marathon field
  • which U.S. states produce the fastest runners in this sample?

Age and performance

1.1. Peak performance by age

age_perf <- nyc_marathon_cleaned %>%
  filter(!is.na(age)) %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(
    runners = n(),
    avg_time = mean(OverallTime_min, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_age_grade = mean(ageGradePercent, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  filter(runners >= 10)

best_ages <- age_perf %>% arrange(avg_time) %>% slice_head(n = 5) 

best_ages %>% kable(caption = "Best average finish times by age")
Best average finish times by age

Calculating average finish time and average age-grade by exact age, then extracts the fastest ages. It provides the base summary for the age-performance discussion.

age_perf %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = age)) +
    geom_line(aes(y = avg_time), color = "#1b9e77", size = 1) +
    geom_point(aes(y = avg_time), color = "#1b9e77", size = 1.5) +
    geom_line(aes(y = avg_age_grade * 2.6), color = "#d95f02", size = 1) +
    scale_y_continuous(
        name = "Average finish time (minutes)",
        sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / 2.6, name = "Average age-grade (%)")
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "Average NYC Marathon finish time and age-grade by runner age",
        x = "Age",
        caption = "Age-grade is shown on the secondary axis to compare relative performance trends"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

The chart above shows that the fastest average finish times occur in the late 20s to early 30s. In this dataset, the lowest average times are concentrated around ages 24-29.

library(countrycode)
library(maps)

Quick Reflexion:

After working with both R and Tableau, I found that Tableau is especially powerful for fast, interactive visualizations. It makes filtering, slicing, and exploring data very intuitive when the goal is to build or iterate on plots quickly. R, however, is stronger for rigorous statistical transformation and reproducible analysis, which makes it the better tool for deeper analytical work.

LLM Integration & Discussion

LLMs were integrated as coding and reasoning assistants during both Data Wrangling (DW) and Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA). The main model used was GPT-5.3 (OpenAI 2026) through Copilot Pro in Visual Studio Code (GitHub Copilot 2026; Microsoft 2026). In practice, Copilot was used to accelerate repetitive coding tasks, propose transformation logic, and help structure exploratory analyses, while final decisions remained under human control.

Prompting strategies

Two prompting strategies were especially useful in this workflow:

  1. Chain-of-thought style prompting (process-focused prompts)
    • Prompts asked the model to reason step-by-step before generating code (for example: inspect schema -> identify potential anomalies -> propose cleaning rules -> provide R code).
    • This improved transparency and made it easier to detect logic errors before execution.
  2. Few-shot prompting (example-guided prompts)
    • Small examples of desired transformations were provided, then the model was asked to generalize (for example, create a engineered feature called “age_group” by using the variable “age”. The format is the following: age < 20, then “Under 20” or age >= 20 & age < 30, then “20-29”).
    • This was useful for keeping goals clear as LLMs sometimes don´t generate what you want.

Additional prompt controls that improved quality included explicit constraints such as “use tidyverse only”, “explain step by step”, or “document the code.”

LLM-assisted workflow pipeline

The operational pipeline used for the DW tasks was:

Raw Dataset -> LLM detects anomalies -> LLM suggests tasks -> LLM generates code -> human verifies everything -> R executes transformations -> clean dataset

In implementation terms:

  1. The raw NYC Marathon file was loaded and profiled in R.
  2. GPT-5.3/Copilot flagged potential issues (time format consistency, missingness patterns, redundant variables, category design opportunities).
  3. The model proposed a prioritized task list for cleaning and enrichment.
  4. The model generated candidate R/tidyverse code.
  5. The analyst reviewed each step for semantic correctness and domain plausibility.
  6. Only validated code was executed in R.
  7. Outputs were re-checked with summary statistics, missing-value audits, and spot inspections before exporting the final cleaned CSV.

This human-in-the-loop structure ensured that LLM assistance increased speed without bypassing analytical validation.

Feedback and limitations

What worked well:

  • Speed and productivity: GPT-5.3 in Copilot Pro reduced the time required to draft repetitive wrangling code and plotting scaffolds.
  • Documentation support: It helped convert technical transformations into report-ready explanations.

Observed limitations:

  • Occasional semantic drift: Some suggestions can misinterpret variable meaning (for example, initially reading racesCount as NYC Marathon participations rather than NYRR-system races).
  • Overconfident outputs: The model may present plausible but incorrect assumptions unless prompts enforce verification.
  • Prompt sensitivity: Output quality depends strongly on precise instructions, constraints, and examples.

Overall, the Large Language Model performed best as an accelerator for coding and structured exploration, not as an autonomous analyst. This is aligned with evidence in prior work that LLMs can substantially support data preparation workflows, but still require careful human validation (Jaimovitch-López et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2024; Zhou et al. 2025; Akella and Narayanam 2025).

Conclusion

This project used an LLM-assisted workflow to clean, enrich, and explore the 2024 NYC Marathon results. The wrangling stage standardized time variables, handled missing values, removed redundant fields, and created interpretable features for age, experience, and performance type. The exploratory analysis then showed that peak raw performance is concentrated in the late 20s and early 30s, that moderate race experience is associated with strong results, and that the field is both geographically diverse and strongly international.

From a methodological perspective, the project shows that LLMs can be useful collaborators in data wrangling and analysis planning when they are kept inside a human-validated workflow. They are most valuable for accelerating transformation design, structuring exploratory ideas, and drafting analysis narratives. The final analytical conclusions, however, still come from the cleaned data and the checks performed in R.
